## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An element $x\in S_n$ and a simple reflection $s$ with $xs<x$ (a right descent), the indecomposable $M=B_x^R$, the generator $B_s^R=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$, the hypothesis $\mathrm{S}(x)$ (so $\operatorname{ch}(M)=\underline H_x$), and the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ on $MB_s$ ([[def-the-deformed-lefschetz-operator-on-b-x-b-s]]).

[F1] Under $\mathrm{S}(x)$ the comparison lemma gives $\operatorname{End}^0(M)=\mathbb R$, the decomposition $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$ with no other summands, and the following structure of $M$: its lowest degree $-\ell(x)$ is one-dimensional, $M$ is finite free as a right $S$-module, and $M$ is self-dual ([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).

[F2] In the decomposition $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ the four maps $\iota_1(r)=r$, $\iota_2(r)=(\alpha_s r)/2$, $\pi_1(r)=(r+s(r))/2$, $\pi_2(r)=\partial_s(r)$ satisfy $\pi_a\circ\iota_b=\delta_{ab}$ and give the inclusions and projections of an $S^s$-bimodule decomposition of $S$; moreover $\alpha_s$ acts on $S$ by an injective map and $s(\alpha_s)=-\alpha_s$ ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]], [[def-the-deformed-lefschetz-operator-on-b-x-b-s]]).

[F3] In the Hecke algebra the right-descent multiplication is $\underline H_x\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_x$ when $xs<x$, and the character of $B_s$ is $\underline H_s$ ([[thm-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-multiplication-formula]]).

## Statement

Let $M=B_x^R$ over $S$ and let $s$ be a right descent, $xs<x$. Assume $\mathrm{S}(x)$. Then there is a graded $(S,S^s)$-bimodule $N$ and an isomorphism $M\cong N\otimes_{S^s}S$. Consequently $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$; choosing the decomposition $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ in the middle tensor factor, the reduced operator $L_\zeta$ has, with respect to the resulting identification $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, the matrix
$$L_\zeta=\begin{pmatrix}\rho\cdot(-)&0\\ \zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)&\rho\cdot(-)\end{pmatrix},$$
where the scalar off-diagonal entry is a degree-two map $M(1)\to M(-1)$. The construction requires no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$. If $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ also holds and $\zeta>0$, this matrix satisfies centered hard Lefschetz; at $\zeta=0$ it fails centered hard Lefschetz.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** construct the descent isomorphism from a split counit, then compute the matrix and the Lefschetz strings.

1.1 **A genuine bimodule section.** Put $U=M\otimes_{S^s}S$, so $MB_s=U(1)$. The actual bimodule decomposition of [F1] gives $U\cong M\oplus M(-2)$. The multiplication counit $c:U\to M$, $c(b\otimes r)=br$, is an $S$-bimodule map. The bottom degree of $U$ is the single line $M^{-\ell(x)}\otimes1$, on which $c$ is nonzero. Only the unshifted summand $M$ in this decomposition has that degree, so $c$ restricts to a nonzero degree-zero endomorphism of that summand. By [F1] it is a nonzero scalar, hence invertible. Compose its inverse with the actual bimodule inclusion to obtain a degree-zero bimodule section $\sigma:M\to U$. On the bottom line $\sigma(b)=b\otimes1$, because $c\sigma=1$ and that line in $U$ is one dimensional. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The twisted counit.** Define $c_s:U\to M_s$ by $c_s(b\otimes r)=b\,s(r)$. It is balanced over $S^s$, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. Since the section $\sigma$ in step 1.1 is genuinely right-$S$-linear, $t=c_s\sigma:M\to M$ is degree zero, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. It is the identity on the bottom line by step 1.1. This argument uses the actual bimodule summand, rather than the generally non-right-linear map $b\mapsto b\otimes1$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 **The involution property of $t$.** Since $t$ is right-$s$-semilinear and degree zero, $t^2$ is an ordinary degree-zero $S$-bimodule endomorphism of $M$, hence a scalar by $\operatorname{End}^0(M)=\mathbb R$; its scalar is $1$ because $t^2$ acts as the identity on the one-dimensional bottom degree by step 2.1. Hence $t^2=\mathrm{id}_M$. [step 2.1, F1]

4.1 **The descent isomorphism.** For $u\in U$ one has $c_s(u)-c(u)\in M\alpha_s$, because $s(r)-r\in\alpha_s S$ for every $r\in S$; consequently $t(m)-m\in M\alpha_s$ for every $m\in M$. Define $N:=\{m\in M: t(m)=m\}$. Every $m$ splits as $m=\tfrac12(m+t(m))+\tfrac12(m-t(m))$ into an invariant and an anti-invariant part, and an anti-invariant $m$ (that is, $t(m)=-m$) lies in $M\alpha_s$, say $m=n\alpha_s$; since right multiplication by $\alpha_s$ is injective by [F2] and $t(m)=-m$ with $s(\alpha_s)=-\alpha_s$ gives $t(n\alpha_s)=t(n)s(\alpha_s)=-t(n)\alpha_s$ and hence $t(n)=n$, we get $n\in N$ and the anti-invariant part of $m$ is $N\alpha_s$. Therefore $M=N\oplus N\alpha_s$ as $(S,S^s)$-bimodules, and the multiplication map induces an isomorphism $N\otimes_{S^s}S\to M$; this proves the descent isomorphism. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2]

5.1 **The matrix of $L_\zeta$.** Use the proved descent $M=N\otimes_{S^s}S$ to write $MB_s=N\otimes_{S^s}S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$. Splitting the middle factor by $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ gives the bimodule isomorphism $MB_s\cong M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, with structure maps $\iota_1,\iota_2,\pi_1,\pi_2$ of [F2] satisfying $\pi_a\iota_b=\delta_{ab}$. In this basis, middle multiplication by $\rho$ has entries $\pi_1(\rho)$, $\pi_1(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and $\partial_s(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, and the operators of multiplication by $\rho$ on the two outer factors contribute the same diagonal $\rho\cdot(-)$ on $M(1)$ and $M(-1)$. All entries except the off-diagonal $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ have positive polynomial degree in $\rho$ and vanish after the right reduction; the off-diagonal entry has the constant term $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and contributes the degree-two map $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee):M(1)\to M(-1)$; hence, after reduction, $L_\zeta$ is the displayed matrix. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, F2, algebra]

6.1 **Hard Lefschetz for $\zeta>0$.** Assume $\mathrm{hL}(x)$, so the reduced module $\overline M$ is a direct sum of centered $\rho$-strings $u_0,\ldots,u_m$ with $\deg u_j=-m+2j$ and $\rho u_j=u_{j+1}$; on each string, left multiplication by $\rho$ is the standard nilpotent Jordan block. In the two-dimensional middle factor with basis $v_-,v_+$ of degrees $-1,+1$ and $e(v_-)=\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)v_+$, $e(v_+)=0$, the operator $e=L_\zeta$ on the string tensor $\bigoplus_j u_j\otimes\{v_-,v_+\}$ acts by $e^k(u_jv_-)=u_{j+k}v_-+k\,u_{j+k-1}v_+$ and $e^k(u_jv_+)=u_{j+k}v_+$ (indices out of range zero), after normalizing the nonzero scalar $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ to $1$ by rescaling $v_+$; for $0\le k\le m-1$ of the compatible parity $k\equiv m+1\pmod2$, in centered degree $-k$ the source basis $u_{(m+1-k)/2}v_-,\,u_{(m-1-k)/2}v_+$ and the corresponding target basis exhibit $e^k$ as a matrix with diagonal entries $1$ and $1$, lower-left entry $k$, and upper-right entry $0$, which is invertible; at $k=m+1$ the map sends $u_0v_-$ to $(m+1)u_mv_+$, nonzero by the normalization $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$. The operator on each string is thus an isomorphism in every centered degree, and $L_\zeta$ on the direct sum of strings satisfies hL. Positivity of $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ uses $\zeta>0$ and strict dominance of $\rho$. [step 5.1, F1, algebra]

7.1 **Failure at $\zeta=0$ and conclusion.** At $\zeta=0$ the matrix of step 5.1 is diagonal with respect to the decomposition $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$. The bottom class $b\in\overline M^{-\ell(x)}$ sits in the first summand in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and satisfies $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}b=0$ because $\overline M^{\ell(x)+2}=0$; the opposite class in $M(-1)$ of degree $\ell(x)+1$ is nonzero by self-duality and dimension symmetry. Hence $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}$ is not injective on $\overline{MB_s}$ in the centered grading and centered hL fails at $\zeta=0$, even though the two individual shifted copies of $\overline M$ have their own strings centered at $\pm1$. Steps 1.1-5.1 prove the descent isomorphism and the matrix, step 6.1 the positive-parameter hard Lefschetz, and this step the failure at zero; no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$ is used. [step 5.1, step 6.1, F1, F3] ∎

## Remarks

- The section $\sigma$ is obtained from the actual bimodule decomposition and the scalar counit restriction on its unshifted summand, so the construction is genuinely a consequence of $\mathrm{S}(x)$ through the comparison lemma, not of an imported singular-descent theorem.
- The off-diagonal entry is a scalar $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ because the middle tensor factor is two-dimensional with a one-dimensional off-diagonal block; no further structure of $N$ enters the computation of the matrix.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote: Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
**The operator.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$, a strictly dominant
$\rho\in S_2$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]])
and a real parameter $\zeta\ge0$. On the tensor product
$B_x^RB_s^R=B_x^R\otimes_SB_s^R$ define
$$L_\zeta:=(\rho\cdot(-))\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B_s^R}+\mathrm{id}_{B_x^R}\otimes(\zeta\,\rho\cdot(-)),$$
where the first summand is left multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor and
the second summand is left multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the second factor.
Because the polynomial ring is commutative and the balanced tensor product
identifies $b r\otimes c=b\otimes rc$ for $r\in S$, the second summand equals
right multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the first factor; both summands are
degree-two, $S$-linear on the right, and commute, so $L_\zeta$ is a degree-two
right-$S$-linear endomorphism of $B_x^RB_s^R$. In particular $L_\zeta$ preserves
the submodule $MS_+$ for $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$\mathbb R$-linear endomorphism of the reduced module
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ ([[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]
supplies the induced invariant form and the reduction conventions of
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]] apply).

**Symmetry.** Each summand of $L_\zeta$ is multiplication by an element in the
commutative position algebra of the tensor product: the first is multiplication
by $\rho$ on the first factor, the second is right (equivalently middle)
multiplication by $\zeta\rho$, which is self-adjoint for the induced invariant
form by the invariance identities of the form. Hence $L_\zeta$ is symmetric for
the induced form, and the Lefschetz forms $(\ ,\ )^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ and the
primitive subspaces $P^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ are those of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]] for this
operator.

**The deformation statements.** Write $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$,
$\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ for centered hard
Lefschetz, the Hodge-Riemann relations and the strong embedded-form statement on
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ for the operator $L_\zeta$, with the bottom degree
$-\ell(x)-1$ and the standard sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ of the dictionary in
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]; the
definitions of $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form respectively to all choices of such forms.
At $\zeta=0$ the operator $L_0=\rho\cdot(-)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is left
multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor, so the zero-parameter statements
$\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ are exactly
the undeformed statements $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$,
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ of the dictionary. For fixed data the family
$\zeta\mapsto L_\zeta$ is polynomial of degree one in $\zeta$.

**Summand stability.** Any direct summand $B\subseteq B_x^RB_s^R$ that is a
sub-bimodule is stable under $L_0$, because left multiplication by the central
element $\rho$ is a bimodule endomorphism; stability under $L_\zeta$ for
$\zeta>0$ is a separate condition, since a projector onto $B$ need not commute
with the middle-position operator. The undeformed summand implications used in
the induction of this page are supplied by the local restriction lemma later on
this page, after deforming the parameter back to $\zeta=0$; no statement of this
definition identifies a restricted positive-parameter operator with a
restriction of $L_\zeta$.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote: Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $w\in S_n$. In the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis $\{\underline H_w\}$ of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]: $$\underline H_s\,\underline H_w=\begin{cases}(v+v^{-1})\,\underline H_w,&sw<w,\\[2pt] \underline H_{sw}+\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{z\in S_n\\ sz<z<w}}\mu(z,w)\,\underline H_z,&sw>w,\end{cases}$$ and symmetrically $\underline H_w\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_w$ if $ws<w$, $\underline H_w\underline H_s=\underline H_{ws}+\sum_{zs<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$ if $ws>w$. Here $\mu(z,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{z,w}$ ([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), which can be nonzero only when $\ell(w)-\ell(z)$ is odd; the sums are finite since $S_n$ is finite. In particular $\underline H_s\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_s$, and $\underline H_s\underline H_w=\underline H_{sw}$ when $sw>w$ and $\ell(w)\le1$. The span conclusion is for the ascent case $sw>w$: there, $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ lies in the span of $\underline H_{sw}$ and of the $\underline H_z$ with $z<w$ and $sz<z$.

reviews.local_disposition: Checked all seven current steps against finite-free, intrinsic support, reflection top-image and flagged Hom supplier interfaces. Finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphisms give locality by polynomial idempotents; finite rank bounds the splitting process. The reduced-word top graph selects one candidate. Maps to the maximal graph quotient and from the graph submodule lift through the two actual Hom-exact flag sequences; their composite is identity on the nonzero top graph, hence nonnilpotent and invertible in the local endomorphism ring. This supplies the split summand, shift uniqueness and residue field without a KL character assumption. Empty word is the unit and the zero object requires no maximal support selection. Local owner completion review only; later independent engine review is unchanged.

## Statement

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The idempotent-complete finite additive tensor category of type-A Bott-Samelson bimodules, over either field, with shifts $M(d)_i=M_{i+d}$ ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]).

[F1] Words are finite free on either side, and their summands are graded free; all fixed-degree Hom spaces are finite-dimensional, because morphisms are determined by finitely many homogeneous generator images in finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]], [[thm-the-type-a-soergel-hom-formula]]).

[F2] Both flags and their canonical Bruhat layers are intrinsic and pass to summands. If $x$ is maximal in the support of $M$, its $x$ graph is the top layer in a compatible enumeration; its inclusion and quotient satisfy $\Gamma_xM\cong\Gamma^xM\,p_x$. Both graph modules are free, and the same identification holds for a summand of a reduced word ([[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]], [[lem-type-a-top-support-layers-are-controlled-by-reflection-localization]]).

[F3] The flagged Hom formula is proved for a flagged source and a Soergel target, and for a Soergel source and a flagged target. For a canonical flag extension its Hom sequence is short exact: prove this degree by degree for word carriers from the three graded Hom rank formulas, and then project to the carrier idempotent ([[thm-the-type-a-soergel-hom-formula]]).

[F4] The flag recursion gives support of a word among its subexpressions. A reduced word of length $m$ for $x$ has its $x$ layer exactly $\Delta_x$, since the only subexpression of product $x$ has all $m$ letters, with generator degree $m$ ([[lem-bott-samelson-bimodules-have-delta-and-nabla-support-filtrations]]).

## Proof

1.1 A finite-dimensional endomorphism algebra and the absence of nontrivial idempotents imply locality. Indeed for an endomorphism $f$ its polynomial minimal relation splits into a power of $T$ and a factor coprime to $T$. The polynomial Chinese remainder identity produces an idempotent separating the nilpotent and invertible parts; indecomposability forces one part to vanish. Thus every $f$ is invertible or nilpotent, and a nonunit $f$ has $1-f$ invertible. Nonunits form a two-sided ideal: multiplication cannot make a nonunit invertible in a finite-dimensional algebra; if two nonunits summed to a unit, dividing their sum would express $1$ as two nonunits, contradicting the invertibility of $1-f$. This is the unique maximal ideal. Its powers eventually vanish: if a power stabilizes, take a minimal finite generating list for that stable ideal and express its last generator using coefficients in the maximal ideal; the invertibility of $1-a$ for such a coefficient eliminates that generator, a contradiction. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Split idempotents until indecomposable summands remain. Each split reduces the positive right rank of its summand, so there are only finitely many splits. The resulting summands have local endomorphism rings by step 1.1. Decompositions are unique: in two finite decompositions, express the identity of one indecomposable as the sum of its composites through the summands of the other. The local maximal ideal cannot contain every composite; an invertible composite gives a split inclusion into one indecomposable summand, hence an isomorphism to it. Remove the common summand and repeat. This proves finite Krull-Schmidt existence and uniqueness. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Decompose a reduced word for $x$. Its top layer is a single $\Delta_x$ by [F4], and the top-layer functor is additive by [F2]. Exactly one indecomposable summand therefore has this graph, with precisely this normalized layer; call it $B_x$. All other summands have support strictly below $x$. This constructs a normalized candidate without any character conjecture. [F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $M$ be any nonzero Soergel object and choose a maximal support label $x$. The two graph layers $\Gamma_xM$ and $\Gamma^xM$ are identified by multiplication by $p_x$ as in [F2]. Choose one homogeneous basis element $m$ of the latter, and let $d$ make its degree equal to the generator degree of $\Gamma^xB_x(d)$. Choose graph maps $f_0:\Gamma^xB_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$ taking that generator to $m$, and $g_0:\Gamma_xM\to\Gamma_xB_x(d)$ which takes the corresponding element $p_xm$ to the generator $p_xb$ and kills the other basis elements. These maps are homogeneous of degree zero and satisfy the identity on the rank-one $x$ layer. [F2, step 3.1, choose]

5.1 Lift these maps to bimodule maps $f:B_x(d)\to M$ and $g:M\to B_x(d)$. The quotient map $M\to\Gamma^xM$ is the last step of a $\nabla$ flag with $x$ last; its kernel is flagged, so [F3] lifts the map $B_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$. The inclusion $\Gamma_xM\to M$ is the first step of a $\Delta$ flag with $x$ first; its quotient is flagged, so [F3] lifts $g_0$ followed by $\Gamma_xB_x(d)\to B_x(d)$. The first lifted map on the quotient and the second on the submodule agree with the prescribed graph maps. The image identity $\Gamma_xM=\Gamma^xM p_x$ makes their composite $gf$ act as the identity on $\Gamma_xB_x(d)$. Thus $gf$ is not nilpotent, and is invertible by step 1.1. Rescale $g$ by its inverse to exhibit $B_x(d)$ as a summand of $M$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1]

6.1 If $M$ is indecomposable, step 5.1 gives $M\cong B_x(d)$. If two normalized candidates were obtained from different reduced expressions for $x$, applying that same splitting argument to either candidate makes them isomorphic, because their normalized rank-one top degrees force $d=0$. Distinct labels cannot be isomorphic, by their maximal support; distinct shifts at a fixed label cannot be isomorphic, by their top generator degrees. This proves classification and reduced-word independence. [step 3.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Restriction of degree-zero endomorphisms of $B_x$ to its rank-one top layer is a unital homomorphism onto $k$, since homogeneous scalars act there and its endomorphism ring in degree zero is $k$. Its kernel is a maximal ideal. Locality in step 1.1 makes this the unique maximal ideal, so the residue field is $k$. All selections were from finite supports and finite homogeneous bases, and no choice axiom beyond finite choice is used. The statement follows from steps 2.1, 3.1, 6.1 and this residue calculation. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1] ∎

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then
   $(M:\Delta_x(d))=(M':\Delta_x(d))+(M'':\Delta_x(d))$ and likewise for
   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
Let $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ be a word in simple reflections and
$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$, with
$B_\emptyset=R$. Then $B_{\underline i}$ belongs to both $F_\Delta$ and
$F_\nabla$: it has a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag in the sense of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], its
support is contained in $Gr(S_n)$, and each successive quotient of these flags
is a standard bimodule $R_x\{a\}$ with $x$ a product
$x=s_{i_{j_1}}\cdots s_{i_{j_m}}$ ($1\le j_1<\cdots<j_m\le r$) of a
subexpression of $\underline i$ formed by keeping $m$ letters; the Coxeter
length $\ell(x)$ can be smaller than $m$. The shift $a$ of an occurrence
is computed recursively, one step $\pm1$ per letter of $\underline i$, from the
two rank-one exact sequences of step 1.2 below: the $\Delta$-chart and the
$\nabla$-chart use the two different sequences, so the shift depends on the
chosen subexpression and on the chart, and it is *not* a function of the lengths
and descent numbers of the subexpression alone: for the one-letter word $(s)$
the $\nabla$-chart occurrences are $R\{1\}$ and $R_s\{-1\}$, while the
$\Delta$-chart occurrences are the translates $\Delta_e(1)=R\{-1\}$ and
$\Delta_s(0)=R_s\{1\}$ of the same two subexpressions, so the same subexpression
carries different shifts in the two charts. In particular the number of occurrences of a graph $x$ in the
$\Delta$-flag and in the $\nabla$-flag of $B_{\underline i}$ is the number of
subexpressions of $\underline i$ with product $x$. Moreover $B_{\underline i}$
is finite free of rank $2^r$ as a left
$R$-module and as a right $R$-module, and the flag categories are closed under
tensoring with a generator on either side: if $M\in F_\Delta$ then
$B_s\otimes_RM\in F_\Delta$ and $M\otimes_RB_s\in F_\Delta$, and likewise with
$\nabla$ in place of $\Delta$.

reviews.local_disposition: Checked the four current steps against the top-support classification and rank-two finite-free interfaces. The induced rank-one pairing has the triangular unit-determinant matrix in a right basis and its dual basis, so word forms are perfect. Right duality preserves fraction-field graph eigencharacters and indecomposability; classification identifies the unique unshifted top summand. Word generator bounds and parity survive split reduction. Evaluation on the top graph sends the single bottom tensor to 1, forcing its nonzero top-summand projection; duality supplies the opposite extremal dimension. No character conjecture or Lefschetz result is used. Local owner completion review only, with no independent audit or invented workflow coverage.

## Statement

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The coordinate type-A realization, the normalized indecomposables $B_x$ and shifts as in [[lem-indecomposable-type-a-soergel-bimodules-are-classified-by-top-support]], and finite right-free bimodules over $R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.

[F1] The normalized $B_x$ is the unique indecomposable summand with the $x$ graph of a reduced word, independent of the word. Its top quotient $\Gamma^xB_x$ is rank one with generator degree $-\ell(x)$, by the image equality and its top $\Delta_x$ layer ([[lem-indecomposable-type-a-soergel-bimodules-are-classified-by-top-support]], [[lem-type-a-top-support-layers-are-controlled-by-reflection-localization]]).

[F2] In $B_s$, the right basis $c_{\mathrm{id}}=1\otimes1$, $c_s=(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s)/2$ has degrees $-1,1$, and satisfies $r c_s=c_s r$ and $r c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}}s(r)+c_s\partial_s(r)$; the generator is finite free on either side ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], [[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).

## Proof

1.1 The unit has the perfect multiplication form. If a right-free bimodule $M$ has an invariant form, put $a(b)=b c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $b(b')=b'c_s$ in $MB_s$ and define the induced form by $\langle a(u),a(v)\rangle=\partial_s\langle u,v\rangle$, $\langle a(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle b(u),a(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle$, and $\langle b(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle\alpha_s$. Extend on a right basis by right bilinearity. The relation of [F2] and the identity $\partial_s(fr)=\partial_s(f)r+s(f)\partial_s(r)$ verify that these formulas agree for arbitrary $u,v$, and that left multiplication is self-adjoint. Symmetry follows from symmetry of the preceding form. If $e_i,e_i^*$ are dual right bases for that form, the pairing between bases $(a(e_i),b(e_i))$ and $(b(e_i^*),a(e_i^*))$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\\alpha_sI&I\end{pmatrix}$, using $\partial_s(1)=0$, and has determinant one. Thus perfection is preserved. Iteration yields a perfect symmetric invariant form on every word, exactly its successive rank-one trace multiplication form. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For finite right-free modules the graded double-dual evaluation is an isomorphism, so $D$ is an involutive contravariant equivalence and takes indecomposables to indecomposables. The invariant perfect word form of step 1.1 identifies a word with its right dual. Generic graph support is unchanged by this duality: in a right basis left multiplication matrices transpose under $D$, so their simultaneous eigencharacters, and hence the graph labels after passing to the polynomial fraction field, are unchanged. A right-free summand has precisely the support closure of those graph labels. Therefore $DB_x$ is an indecomposable summand with the $x$ graph of the same reduced word. Uniqueness in [F1] identifies it with $B_x$ with no shift. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A word of length $m$ has a homogeneous right basis given by tensor products of the two basis elements in [F2]; its generator degrees lie between $-m$ and $m$ and have parity $m$. Right reduction preserves a split direct-sum decomposition. Since $B_x$ is an unshifted summand of its reduced word of length $m=\ell(x)$, its reduction has these same bounds and parity. The word's bottom degree is the single $1$-tensor. The balanced evaluation of that word on its top graph, obtained by successively twisting the tensor-slot polynomials by the successive prefix permutations, sends this $1$-tensor to $1$. It factors through the rank-one top quotient, and is an isomorphism onto $R_x(m)$ because both generators have degree $-m$. All other summands have no $x$ support; consequently the projection of the bottom tensor into $B_x$ is nonzero. Its bottom dimension is therefore one. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Right duality reverses the degrees of the finite homogeneous basis after reduction. The unshifted duality $DB_x\cong B_x$ from step 2.1 therefore makes the reduced dimensions symmetric and gives top dimension one from the bottom dimension in step 3.1. The perfect trace forms, duality, degree bounds, parity and extremal dimensions have now all been established locally. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

**Scalar extension of the published realization.** The published type-A page
works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations
$w\cdot x_i:=x_{w(i)}$ ([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]).
On this page $\alpha_i$ always means the coordinate root
$\alpha_i:=\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$, and $\alpha_i^\vee:=\beta_i^\vee$ is the
coordinate coroot, so that under the standard form the Cartan entries are
$\langle\alpha_i^\vee,\alpha_j\rangle=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ and
adjacent entries are $-1$; the reflection is
$s_i(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_i\rangle\alpha_i^\vee$. The alternating balanced
roots $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}$ are retained by the published page for its
diagrammatic presentation and are not used for positivity, Demazure traces or
descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of
$\partial_i$ and of the trace.

**The real generators and the real category.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ set
$$B_i^R:=S\otimes_{S^{s_i}}S(1),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(S,S^{s_i})$-bimodule $S$ with the
$(S^{s_i},S)$-bimodule $S$, shifted in the Elias-Williamson convention
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$ used on this page ([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]],
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Its left basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ have degrees $-1$ and $+1$, and
$B_i^R$ is finite free of rank two on each side
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]). The **real
type-A Soergel category** $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is the idempotent completion
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) of the full subcategory of graded
$(S,S)$-bimodules whose objects are the finite direct sums of shifts
$B_{\underline i}^R(d)=B_{i_1}^R\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{i_r}^R(d)$ of real
Bott-Samelson products ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with the
same internal shifts as the rational category, i.e. $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$ in the
Elias-Williamson convention. Its unit is the graded ring $S$ itself, regarded
as an object in cohomological degree zero; it is not a polynomial ring
concentrated in internal degree zero. Categorically,
$\mathrm{SBim}_n^R=\mathrm{Kar}(\mathrm{BSBim}_n^R)$ has the same formal
properties as the rational Soergel category: it is graded, additive,
idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite
direct sum of graded shifts of indecomposables.

**Scalar extension of objects.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ over the
rational polynomial ring put $M^R:=M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, with the
$S$-actions induced from the $R$-actions and the tensor grading. Since
$\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ is flat, scalar extension is exact on graded pieces;
it carries the rational generator $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ to $B_i^R$, the
rational Bott-Samelson construction to the real one, and the rational
idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the
$\Delta$- and $\nabla$-flags with their characters, and all formulas of the
rational page are read over $\mathbb R$ after extension. The Hecke algebra
used for characters is the integral normalized algebra
$H_v(n)$ over $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with basis $H_x$ of
[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same
algebra before and after the scalar extension, since it is defined over
$\mathbb Z$.

**The dominant chamber.** The **dominant chamber** on this page is the set of
strictly dominant degree-two elements
$$\Theta:=\Bigl\{\rho=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\ :\ c_j\in\mathbb R,\ c_j>c_{j+1}\ \text{for } 1\le j\le n-1\Bigr\}\subset S_2 .$$
It is nonempty, for example for $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$, which gives
$c_j-c_{j+1}=1$ for every $j$. For $\rho=\sum_jc_jx_j$ the coordinate
evaluation is $\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)=\rho(x_i-x_{i+1})=c_i-c_{i+1}$, so
$\rho\in\Theta$ is exactly a degree-two element with
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot; no alternating-sign chamber
and no replacement of $\rho$ is used anywhere on this page.

**Conventions.** All tensor products are over $S$ unless indicated, all shifts
are the internal shifts just fixed, "form" on this page always means a graded
symmetric form that is $S$-bilinear for the right action and invariant under
the left action in the sense fixed by the intersection-form definition below, and
dimensions of reduced modules are always real dimensions. The rational
comparison statements needed for labels, characters and forms are collected
in the comparison lemma later on this page.

reviews.local_disposition: Checked four current proof steps and the block, simple-head and semistandard/Kostka interfaces. Central-idempotent projection is exact; a finite-dimensional module with a simple head is indecomposable, so each Weyl class projects to itself or zero. Subtraction of the projected class identity and independence of Weyl classes eliminate every outside-block coefficient. Independence uses the finite unitriangular weight matrix, not an assumed Weyl filtration of an arbitrary module. The zero module case gives all coefficients zero. Local owner repair review only, not independent Alpha execution.

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S=S(d,n)$ be the
$q$-Schur algebra over $F$ with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Let $M$ be a finite
dimensional right $S$-module all of whose composition factors lie in a single
block $B$ of $S$
([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and let integers $a_{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, satisfy
$$[M]=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$$
in the Grothendieck group $G_0(S\text{-mod})$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]). Then
$W^{\lambda}$ lies in $B$ whenever $a_{\lambda}\ne0$. In particular no nonzero
virtual combination of Weyl classes all of whose terms lie outside $B$ can
equal the class of a module in $B$.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, the algebra $S=S(d,n)$ with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, a finite dimensional right $S$-module $M$ whose composition factors all lie in one block $B$, and integers $a_{\lambda}$ with $[M]=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$ in $G_0(S\text{-mod})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]).

[F1] Blocks: $1=\sum_i\epsilon_i$ is the unique decomposition of the identity of $S$ into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents, the blocks are the two-sided ideals $B_i=S\epsilon_i=\epsilon_iS$, and for every right $S$-module $N$ one has $N=\bigoplus_iN\epsilon_i$; a simple module $L$ lies in exactly one block and satisfies $L\epsilon_i=L$ for that $i$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]). We write $\epsilon_B$ for the idempotent of the block $B$ of the statement.

[F2] Each Weyl module has nonzero simple head $L^\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

[F3] The proof of [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]], steps 1.1 and 3.1, gives additive weight dimensions and the weight matrix $K_{\lambda\nu}=\dim(W^\lambda1_\nu)$. This matrix, restricted to partitions with at most $d$ parts, is unitriangular and hence invertible by [[lem-kostka-change-of-basis-is-dominance-unitriangular]]. Applying these dimensions to a zero virtual Weyl combination forces every coefficient to vanish. This proves the linear independence used here; no Weyl filtration of an arbitrary module is assumed.

[F4] An exact functor between abelian categories induces a homomorphism of Grothendieck groups, and the finite-dimensional $S$-modules form an abelian category in which $G_0$ is computed by composition multiplicities ([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]).

## Proof


**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Multiplication by the central idempotent $\epsilon_B$ is the projection of every right $S$-module onto its $B$-summand: $N=\bigoplus_iN\epsilon_i$ by [F1], so $N\epsilon_B$ is that direct summand and is a submodule, and $N\epsilon_B=N$ exactly when all composition factors of $N$ lie in $B$. The assignment $N\mapsto N\epsilon_B$ is exact, because it is the projection onto a direct summand of the identity functor: for $f:N\to N'$ one has $f(N\epsilon_B)=f(N)\epsilon_B$, $\ker(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\ker f)\epsilon_B$ and $\operatorname{im}(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\operatorname{im}f)\epsilon_B$, so it preserves kernels and images. [F1, F4]

1.2 A nonzero finite-dimensional module has a simple quotient: choose a proper submodule of maximal vector-space dimension. If a Weyl module had two nonzero summands, each would have a nonzero head, so its head would not be simple, contrary to [F2]. Thus it is indecomposable. Its block decomposition [F1] has precisely one nonzero summand, the block containing its head $L^\lambda$; hence $W^\lambda\epsilon_B$ is either $W^\lambda$ or $0$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Apply the exact projection of step 1.1 to the class identity of the hypothesis. Since $M\epsilon_B=M$ by the hypothesis that all composition factors of $M$ lie in $B$, and since $W^{\lambda}\epsilon_B$ is $W^{\lambda}$ or $0$ by step 1.2, the induced identity in $G_0$ reads $$[M]=\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\in B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}].$$ Subtracting it from the given identity $[M]=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$ yields $$\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\notin B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]=0$$ in $G_0(S\text{-mod})$. [F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By the linear independence of the Weyl classes [F3], all coefficients in the vanishing combination of step 2.1 are zero: $a_{\lambda}=0$ for every $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}\notin B$, which is the contrapositive of the assertion that $a_{\lambda}\ne0$ implies $W^{\lambda}\in B$. [F3, step 2.1] ∎

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $n\ge0$ and $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently, for finite $e$, the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. For $e=\infty$ we set $C_\infty(\lambda):=\lambda$; the algebra is semisimple and its blocks are indexed by the partitions of $n$.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, parameter $q$, quantum characteristic $e$, integer $d\ge n$, and the Weyl modules in the statement. Write $S=S_F(d,n)$ and $W^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}_F$.

[F1] The semistandard cellular basis has cells $W^{\lambda}$, nonzero absolutely simple heads $L^{\lambda}$, and dominance-unitriangular decomposition multiplicities $d_{\lambda\mu}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The cellular anti-involution induces contragredient duality fixing the simple isomorphism classes, through the nondegenerate cell form on each simple head ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The balanced hook-ratio Jantzen formula and alternating beta symbols ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]) use conjugate beta numbers $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+N-j$, with $N$ sufficiently large, and read $$\sum_{r>0}[W^{\lambda}(r)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(v(h^{\lambda}_{ab})-v(h^{\lambda}_{ac})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}],$$ where $W^{\lambda}(r)$ are filtration submodules, $W^{\lambda}(1)=\operatorname{rad}W^{\lambda}$, and the right hand symbols are zero on repeated or negative entries and otherwise have the sign of sorting the beta sequence. The suppliers must carry this balanced form; the earlier displayed unbalanced manuscript indices do not preserve degree.

[F3] Core abaci are obtained by packing beads upwards on each runner, so their shapes depend only on runner bead counts; rim-hook removal is a bead-to-gap move ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Conjugation reverses dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]). Transposing every strip in a maximal $e$-hook removal sequence gives such a sequence for the conjugate partition; hook lengths are preserved by transposition, so its terminal core is the conjugate core. Hence $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\lambda)'$.

[F4] Primitive central idempotents decompose the identity, and every finite-dimensional module splits into their block summands ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]). Weyl classes are linearly independent in the Grothendieck group, so a nonzero accumulated Weyl coefficient in the class of a module supported in one block forces that Weyl module into the block ([[lem-virtual-weyl-combinations-detect-q-schur-block-separation]], [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]).



[F5] The radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is nilpotent and its quotient semisimple ([[thm-jacobson-radical-is-nilpotent-and-the-quotient-is-semisimple]]); the Wedderburn decomposition is a product of matrix rings over division rings ([[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]]). Cellular ideal layers are the tensor products of the contragredient left cell and the right cell ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. For $n=0$, $S_F(d,0)=F$, with its one empty-label module, so all assertions hold directly; hence assume $n>0$. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Composition-factor cores. An off-head simple occurs in $W^{\lambda}$ exactly when it occurs in its radical, equivalently in the positive Jantzen sum: the first submodule is the radical and every later one is contained in it. Its nonzero multiplicity in that sum implies it occurs in some $W^{\mu}$ with $J_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, since otherwise its coefficient in the sum would be zero. Step 2.1 gives the same core and strict dominance descent. Induction on the finite dominance poset proves that every factor $L^{\nu}$ of $W^{\lambda}$ has $C_e(\nu)=C_e(\lambda)$. No identity equating the radical class with the positive sum is asserted. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical. [F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. By [F5] and the absolute simplicity in [F1], the semisimple quotient is a product of full matrix rings over $F$. Lift its matrix diagonal idempotents: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ changes an error $a=u^2-u$ to $-3a^2+4a^3$, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_\nu$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_\nu=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda\nu}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Assume $e<\infty$. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, with $l=\ell(\gamma)$, and set $\rho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu\ne\rho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=\rho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $\nu$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $\nu$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows. [F3, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 The bridge coefficients are nonzero. Write $l=\ell(\mu)=\ell(\sigma)$. If $i>1$, then $\sigma_1=\mu_1$ and the row1 hook pair in $\nu$ at columns $j,\mu_1+1$ has lengths $A=h^{\mu}_{1j}$ and $h$: the first is nondivisible because row1 precedes the first divisible row, and the second is divisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\mu$, so its coefficient is nonzero. If $i=1$, then $\sigma_1=j-1$, and the row1 pair at columns $j,j+1$ has lengths $h,h-1$; its balanced transfer $h-1$ sorts to $\mu$, again giving a nonzero coefficient. For $\eta$, the pair at columns $1,\sigma_1+1$ has lengths $A'=\sigma_1+h+l-1$ and $h$. When $i>1$, $A'-h^{\mu}_{i1}=A$, so $A'$ is nondivisible; when $i=1$, $A'=h^{\mu}_{11}+h-1$, also nondivisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\eta$. Each claimed target has precisely two lost and two gained beta values, so the uniqueness argument in step 2.2 rules out cancellation. Thus both $J_{\nu\mu}$ and $J_{\nu\eta}$ are nonzero. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 6.1] ∎

## Remarks

The connectivity argument follows the corrected dominance-minimum route of Lyle–Mathas Proposition 3.7 and Corollary 4.3, while proving the needed elementary row properties locally. Their final Remark explicitly corrects the earlier first-row-only q-Schur argument; the old direct hook move can have zero coefficient.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis
$(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$
there is a unique $R$-bilinear form
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$
with
$$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is
independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$
depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric,
$\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative,
$\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$,
where $i(a)y$ denotes the right action $y\,i(a)$ of $i(a)$ on $y$, i.e. the
left action $a\cdot y:=y\,i(a)$; (iii) characterised by
$x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for
$x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$
is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of
$x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $ eta= eta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. 2. u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

supplier_interfaces.contract_quote:
Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and

Definition

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.
